anomaly_def.Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Mis-tuned engine parameters (memory pools, checkpoint cadence, parallelism limits, etc.) create artificial pressure or idle gaps that do not reflect the true hardware capacity.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical pages or index structures on disk become internally inconsistent or corrupted, making stored data and access paths unreliable.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume an abnormally large share of CPU cycles, driving the host to sustained compute saturation.

Combined phenomena: The instance shows near-100 % CPU utilisation, long run-queues, and pervasive scheduler waits while I/O devices oscillate between bursts and idle periods. Queries that once used indexes fall back to full scans or repeatedly re-read pages after failed checksum validations, inflating CPU usage and causing erratic latency spikes. Frequent checkpoints or aggressive background verification jobs—triggered by tight configuration thresholds—collide with corruption-induced page rereads, producing log-flush storms and lock contention. Monitoring highlights mismatches between hardware utilisation (CPU pegged, disks underused) and wait-event mixes that include CPU spin waits, page verification failures, and redo-flush pressure. Application symptoms range from sporadic “page corruption” or “could not read block” errors to global slow-downs as the engine burns CPU retrying failed I/O and running mis-sized maintenance tasks.

Causal chain: 1) Misconfigured memory and checkpoint parameters shrink buffer pools or force excessively frequent flushes, magnifying I/O churn and the probability that latent page or index corruption is touched. 2) Encountering corrupted structures causes the optimizer to abandon indexes or to invoke page-verification and error-recovery code paths that are markedly CPU-intensive. 3) The unexpected CPU demand pushes the host into saturation; with parallelism caps set too high, additional worker threads compete for already scarce cycles, further amplifying CPU waits. 4) High CPU load slows checkpoint completion and recovery threads, extending the window in which partially flushed or torn pages can propagate, potentially worsening corruption. Thus, mis-tuned configuration, latent storage corruption, and compute exhaustion create a self-reinforcing loop that degrades performance, increases error rates, and jeopardizes data integrity across both transactional and analytical workloads.

entry.official_definition: The length of time in seconds an InnoDB transaction waits for a row lock before giving up.
entry.trigger_condition: An InnoDB transaction waits longer than innodb_lock_wait_timeout for a row lock.
entry.workload_impact: The lock wait gives up; by default only the current statement is rolled back unless innodb_rollback_on_timeout is enabled.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as an InnoDB system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
